skill.name: Crew writing jobs: a news report, a persuasive letter, an exposé
skill.why: Each writing job has a purpose: inform, persuade or reveal the truth.
skill.how: News answers who, what, when and where. Letters give reasons. Exposés show the proof.

steps.say: The crew has three writing jobs. First, a news report. Readers want the facts, fast.

show.nudge: That's when it happened. Which part tells you where?
That's who it happened to. Which part tells you where?
That's what happened. Which part tells you where?

steps.ask: Tap the part that tells you where it happened.
steps.win: Yes! One line gives who, what, when and where. A news report informs, straight away.

steps.say: Second job: a persuasive letter. Now I want the mayor to do something.

show.text: Please ban drones over the bay,
show.nudge: That's what I want. Find the part that says why.
That's just how I finish the letter. Find the part that says why.

steps.win: Yes! A persuasive letter asks for something and gives reasons. Its job is to persuade.

steps.say: Third job: an exposé. Say it ex-POH-zay. It catches someone telling a lie.

show.text: Maxx says he sets every Creature free.
show.nudge: That's what Maxx says. Which part shows it isn't true?

show.text: Here is a photo of forty Creatures in his cages.

show.nudge: That's how we feel. Which part shows Maxx is lying?

steps.ask: Tap the proof that Maxx is lying.
steps.win: Yes! First his claim, then proof that it is false. An exposé exposes a lie.

steps.say: Zed wrote this and called it an exposé. Careful: exposé sounds like exposition, but they're different jobs.
show: Maxx's stream should be banned, because he is mean and horrible.
steps.ask: What does Zed's line need to be an exposé?

options.reason: Opinions and reasons argue a side. That's an exposition. What does an exposé show?

options.text: proof that Maxx said something false

options.reason: It already has because. Reasons argue. What does an exposé show?

steps.win: Yes! An exposition argues an opinion. An exposé shows proof that someone lied. No proof, no exposé.

steps.say: My desk is a mess. Here are three scraps from three different jobs.

show.nudge: That reports what happened and when. Does it catch a lie?

show.text: Please make lunch longer, because we need to play.
show.nudge: That asks for something and gives a reason. Does it catch a lie?

show.text: Maxx says he sleeps at night. Here's his 2am stream.

steps.ask: Tap the scrap from an exposé.
steps.win: Yes! A claim, then proof that it's false. Look at the labels: three jobs.

steps.say: So first, decide your job. Gus wants the mayor to fix the broken jetty.
steps.ask: Which writing job should Gus pick?

options.reason: News reports what happened. Gus wants the mayor to do something.
Nobody is lying here. Gus wants to change the mayor's mind.

steps.win: Yes! He wants to persuade, so he writes a letter with reasons. Now pick your job: inform, persuade or expose?

terms.means: Informs. Tells who, what, when and where, straight away.
Persuades. Asks someone to do something, and gives reasons.
Exposes a lie with proof. Not an exposition, which argues an opinion.
Photos, facts or records that show if a claim is true.

examples.text: Maxx says his Creatures eat organic food.
Our video shows a bucket of stale chips.
Please ban drones over the bay,

card.test: First ask: am I informing, persuading or exposing a lie? Then give facts, reasons or proof.

weDo.frame: Wren is writing for the crew's news channel.
weDo.prompt: Which is the best opening for a news report?
weDo.hint: News answers who, what, when and where. Which one does?
weDo.success: It tells when, where and what happened, straight away. That's how news reports begin.

options.text: Last night at Inkwell Bay, Maxx Vantablack's boat ran aground on a sandbar.
Dear Mayor, Maxx Vantablack's boat ran aground last night, so please ban it.
options.reason: This starts like a letter to the Mayor. A news report tells everyone what happened, straight away.

options.text: The waves crashed and the wind howled as Maxx's boat crept towards the sand.
options.reason: This sounds like the start of a story. A news report says when and where, straight away.

weDo.frame: Wren's exposé of Maxx has a hole in it.
weDo.prompt: Tap the line that is only Wren's opinion. Then choose the proof that catches Maxx out.
weDo.hint: An exposé puts the claim beside the proof. Which line is only an opinion?
weDo.success: The receipts show Maxx's claim is false. Claim, then proof: that's how an exposé works.

parts.tap: Maxx says his Creatures eat five-star food.
parts.reason: That's Maxx's claim, not Wren's opinion. An exposé needs the claim, so it stays.
Asking readers to act is a strong ending. Find the line that is only an opinion.

options.text: His own receipts show one bag of stale chips since June.
My friend's cousin says she saw his Creatures eating chips.
options.reason: A story from a friend's cousin is hard to check. An exposé shows proof anyone can see.

options.text: Lots of people online think he is lying too.
options.reason: What people think isn't proof. An exposé shows evidence.

creature.name: Beamquid
creature.blurb: A little squid that flashes a beam on anything hidden. Maxx hates it, because it always finds his secret cages.

workshop.mentor:
MAXX'S 'RESCUE CENTRE' IS A CAGE FARM
Maxx Vantablack tells his followers that every Creature he catches goes to a 'five-star rescue centre'. Last Tuesday, our crew went to see it. There was no centre. There was a rusty shed with forty-two cages stacked to the roof, and a padlock on every door.
Maxx says our photos are fake. Then why is the same shed in the background of his own stream?
The Creatures can't speak up. You can.
workshop.ask:
Write five sentences for one job: a letter asking for longer lunch, a news report, or a Maxx exposé.
Stuck? Start with: 'Dear Principal,'
Challenge: answer the other side's argument.
checklist: I picked one job: news, letter or exposé.
My first sentence gives the main fact, ask or claim.
I can point to two facts, reasons or proofs.
I swapped one blurry word (good, bad, stuff).
